groups.name: The action boundary: authorization, containment and egress
groups.scope: Everything that decides whether an agent may act, where it may act and what may leave is being moved out of the model and into machinery the model cannot rewrite: least-privilege capability derivation, per-call authorization at the call site, runtime policy gates and approval flows, effect-bounded lowering of a tool call, budget and workflow-level risk limits, and OS- or kernel-level sandboxes and containment. The confidentiality half of the same boundary belongs here too — secret hygiene, de-identification, confidential inference and egress filtering that decide what data may cross outward — because the adversary and the boundary are the same one: authority and information leaving the agent. The seam with neighbouring themes is that Theme G watches what ran and Theme C records who authorised it; what is settled here is what may execute and what may escape.

groups.name: Evaluation, benchmarking and measurement validity
groups.scope: Almost every claim about agent security reaches the reader through a benchmark, a metric or an adversarial campaign, and this theme is the machinery of that measurement: staged severity rubrics with explicit denominators, contamination-free and leakage-aware designs, blinded and multi-judge grading, harness-as-a-variable ablation, unearned passes, oracle hacking and verifier compromise, and closed-loop red teaming that feeds discovered failures back into the target. The front of work is making security claims auditable rather than assertable — a verification stack for the evaluation itself, including adversarial campaigns run against live defenders and measurement of the harness rather than only the model. It stops at the seam with the mechanisms being measured: injection mechanics sit in Theme A, sandbox escapes in Theme B, monitor reliability in Theme G and code-review agents in Theme D.

groups.name: Untrusted content and poisoned context steering the agent
groups.scope: Content the agent reads is an instruction channel: fetched pages, tool return values, tool and MCP descriptions, retrieved documents, images and error strings are executed as if the operator had said them, while memory, skills, the knowledge base and the retrieval store are written to carry a payload into a later session. The front of work is provenance-typed content and write-gated state — channel enumeration with per-surface contamination measurement, origin typing of observations, preflight sanitization of tool output, memory lifecycle gating at write, retrieval and promotion, and selective repair of poisoned entries — because the model cannot be taught to separate data from instructions. The seam with Theme E is distribution: poisoning that arrives through a third-party skill or MCP package is supply chain, whereas poisoning planted in the agent's own context and memory is context control.

groups.name: Detection and monitoring of autonomous behaviour
groups.scope: Once agents act unattended, their behaviour has to be watched and their claims have to be checked: trace-level misuse detection, procedural auditing of trajectories rather than outcomes, runtime drift monitoring, span-level attribution of which input drove a behaviour, and deception detection that reads behaviour rather than text, including tripwires, canaries and deception environments that catch an attacker by its own actions. The front of work is evidence-grounded observability — verifying the trace rather than the agent's own report — together with the honest accounting of how far monitoring itself can be evaded, how detectors collapse under shift, and how correlated failures make a stacked defence weaker than its parts suggest. The seam with Theme B is that Theme B decides what may run and Theme G decides whether what ran should have.

groups.name: Supply chain and model artifacts
groups.scope: Everything an agent installs, imports or executes is a supply chain: third-party skills, MCP servers and tool packages, the repositories a coding agent reads, the model weights and adapters it runs, and the unguarded update boundary between installation-time and execution-time trust. The front of work is artifact-level trust — poisoned tool descriptions, backdoors with semantic or temporal triggers, screening and marketplace trust derived from declared permissions, attested admission of tool servers, version-level risk propagation, and closing the inspection-execution gap where a scanner reads source while a different artefact actually runs. The seam with Theme A is the reader: content poisoned inside the agent's own environment is context control, whereas the same content arriving through a distributed third-party artefact is supply chain.

groups.name: Identity, delegation, provenance and audit trails
groups.scope: Authority has to be attached to a principal, attenuated along a delegation chain, and recorded in a form that survives the agent: identity-bound approval tokens, per-hop scoped delegation packets, signed and hash-chained evidence chains, tamper-evident receipts, and explicit attribution of which human or agent actually approved which effect. The front of work is an answerable audit trail — proving which artefact a verdict rested on, separating a human approval from an approval an agent submitted under a person's name, and attributing a shared violation back to the actors whose actions caused it. The seam with Theme B is timing: Theme B enforces at the moment of action, this theme produces the principal and the record behind it.

groups.name: Human and organisational response: governance, oversight and incident response
groups.scope: The controls that sit above the agent: layered governance frameworks scaled to the degree of agency, accountability and regulatory mapping with explicit human oversight, repository-hosted governance contracts whose gates refuse to pass without evidence, compliance and assurance gap analysis, and the human loop itself — alert triage and prioritisation, fatigue and warning over-suppression, and the erosion of the very skills oversight depends on. The front of work is organisational rather than technical: whether an organisation can answer for its agents, price their risk, and notice when its own oversight is failing. The seam with Theme J is that this theme is the response machinery, while Theme J is the measured harm that the response is reacting to.

groups.name: Code the agent writes, reviews and repairs
groups.scope: Agents write code that ships: repositories get scanned at scale, generated code carries exploitable patterns and hallucinated dependencies, patches are accepted without verification, and automated repair can introduce fresh vulnerabilities. The front of work is making the agent's output a verified artefact — execution- and review-based validation by a party that did not author it, exploit-guided and verification-gated repair, differential and proof-coupled repair verification, and formal verification or specification-to-implementation gap analysis as the release gate on what the agent produced. The seam with Theme E is the direction of trust — Theme E covers what the agent consumes, this theme covers what the agent authors, reviews and repairs — and the seam with Theme G is that here the review is the control, not a runtime monitor.

groups.name: Measured real-world consequence: offence, economics, availability and safety
groups.scope: What the corpus measures actually happening in the world: autonomous offensive capability end to end and agents that propagate themselves, misuse of personal agents for fraud and social engineering, agent marketplaces substituting human labour, availability and cost attacks that flood context or burn tokens, and intrinsic misalignment that produces unsafe actions with no attacker present at all. The front of work is consequence evidence rather than mechanism — capability and harm measured end to end, priced, and attributed to whoever bears them, so that defensive spend can be argued for. The seam with Theme B is that resource, credential and sandbox controls are mechanisms in Theme B; here the measured object is the harm, its cost and its victims.

groups.name: Multi-agent trust and collusion
groups.scope: Multi-agent pipelines add hops that a single-agent trust model never sees: safe models do not compose into safe pipelines, a compromised peer escalates through a coordinator, an insider shapes the consensus of its neighbours, and harmful work is split so that no single agent's trace looks wrong. The front of work is composition — capability tokens and gated knowledge promotion that fence collaborators by construction, trust-boundary enforcement, credit attribution for a shared violation, anti-collusion incentives, and treating the links between agents as an attack surface in their own right. It is the smallest theme here because in this corpus most multi-agent mechanisms are named inside other fronts — poisoning, egress, monitoring — and the techniques gathered here are the ones that treat the team itself as the adversary.

ranked.technique: Deterministic pre-action authorization at the call site
ranked.mechanism: The authority decision is made by a policy engine the model cannot instruct, and it is made at the moment of invocation, so one canonical policy governs every action surface rather than a per-harness prompt. The engine sees the concrete call — tool, target, arguments, context — and returns allow, deny, ask or throttle; deny is the default, and the model cannot argue for an exception because the check happens outside it. The evidence it consumes is the call itself plus a policy pack (allow/deny rules, argument invariants, cost and rate budgets, approval gates) and, where the platform supports it, a machine-readable assurance level. The rule is fail-closed: an unparseable or malformed call context is a denial rather than a pass. Caution: this control is evaded whenever the check is placed behind the model instead of in front of it — an unscanned engine in one evaluation recorded attack recall 0.000 — and the strongest results depend on the policy being explicit rather than prose; the same study showed that model-level filters (screeners, instruction hierarchies) can be bypassed with 100% attack success.
ranked.reported_results: Under a permissive policy, social engineering succeeded 74.6% of the time, while a restrictive policy held a comparable attacker population to 0% across 879 attempts; median 53 ms over 1,000 authorization decisions, with 4,437 decisions across 1,151 sessions and 173 evaluation_error denials (7.1%) (arxiv:2603.20953). Across 225 controlled runs over five policy packs and three fault profiles, stricter packs raised violation prevention from 0.000 in P0 to 0.681 in P4 while task success fell from 0.356 to 0.067, retry amplification fell from 3.774 to 1.378, and leakage recall reached 0.875 (arxiv:2603.18059). LMSM-Checkpoint reduced HarmBench attack success from 39.20% to 3.32% with false refusals rising 2.40% to 4.40%, retaining 98.14% of throughput (arxiv:2608.25697). APEX attained 0% attack success on five of six benchmarks and 0.56% on the sixth against 13 baselines, and held 0% under adaptive attacks on all three capability-unit types (arxiv:2610.06966). Explicit example-based policy boundaries raised recall 5.5-26.1 points on all 23 models, with one model reaching 98.2% recall and interruptions down from 30.6% to 4.8% at 120 ms median latency (arxiv:2611.02155). Baseline models were already 97.4%-98.2% resistant to syntactically explicit single-turn injections on AgentDojo, SkillInject and MCPSafeBench (arxiv:2604.11790). AgentTrust reached 95.0% detection on 300 production scenarios and 73.7% on a 630-scenario ruleset (96.7% with a patched ruleset, ~93% on obfuscated payloads) (arxiv:2605.04785). A deterministic numeric-grounding verifier caught 60% of failures (96% with the coverage check) at 0 of 63 false positives, against the monitor's 54% at 17 (arxiv:2608.02464). A fail-loudly runtime scored 0.723 with full source retrieval and 0.747 with gold sources on KramaBench, relative gains of 35.9% and 28.8% over the strongest baselines (arxiv:2609.32528). Reviewing combined artifacts reduced a denied-commit rate of 86.0% to zero with no loss of authorized supply, and object binding raised selective correctness from zero to ~99% over 2,304 trials (arxiv:2610.00371). Policy gating and execution filtering on a self-hosted multi-agent deployment reduced compromise probability by 0.10, boundary failures by 0.10 and privilege drift by 0.02 (all p < 0.0001) while task utility fell from 0.93 to 0.89 and median latency rose from 420 ms to 468 ms (arxiv:2606.15008). WASM-sandboxed execution re-ran 33 of 35 scanned MCP tool repositories and observed source-to-sink witnesses in 12 (arxiv:2601.01241). Negative: the unscanned engine recorded accuracy 0.455 and attack recall 0.000 (arxiv:2603.11853).
ranked.trajectory: The direction is a move from model-internal safeguards to a single non-model enforcement point shared by every tool surface, driven by the repeated finding that probabilistic guards are bypassable (one paper reports the combination of StruQ and instruction hierarchy bypassed with 100% attack success, and 12 other probabilistic defences similarly). The indicator would be agent frameworks shipping per-call re-authorization with concrete argument values as a default rather than offering capability gating alone, since an audit of three frameworks found all three provide gating by default and none re-authorize each call. Because the papers also report that policy strictness trades directly against task success (0.356 to 0.067 across packs), expect the trajectory to be measured in utility-adjusted rather than absolute blocking rates.
ranked.defensive_move: Put one policy engine between the model and every tool invocation, and make it the only path to an effect; keep the canonical policy in that engine rather than in per-harness prompts. It must deny any call not explicitly allowed, deny calls whose arguments fall outside the granted scope, and treat an unparseable call context as a denial rather than a pass.
ranked.test_recipe: Replay a fixed corpus of tool calls with concrete arguments through the engine, including calls a model produced under injection and calls that differ only in one argument (payment recipient, host, path), and assert that the deny path fires on each and that every allow is written to an audit log; report the deny rate and the false-deny rate separately.

glm.responsible_owner: the team deploying agents, with platform/infra
glm.rationale: The strongest-evidenced control in the corpus: a restrictive policy held a comparable attacker population to 0% across 879 attempts where a permissive one lost 74.6% (arxiv:2603.20953), and APEX held 0-0.56% ASR across six benchmarks and under adaptive attacks (arxiv:2610.06966). The baseline has no mediated tool boundary — permissions are the developer's, inherited wholesale — so a deny-by-default engine in front of every tool call is the highest-leverage gap closable this quarter. The recorded caution (attack recall 0.000 when the check sits behind the model, and 100% bypass of model-level filters, arxiv:2603.18059) argues for placement at the call site, not against the control.

minimax.rationale: A policy engine outside the model held a comparable attacker population to 0% across 879 attempts and LMSM-Checkpoint cut HarmBench attack success from 39.2% to 3.3% (arxiv:2603.20953, arxiv:2608.25697), while one study recorded attack recall 0.000 for an unscanned engine and 100% bypass of model-level filters (arxiv:2603.11853) - so the check has to sit in front of the call. The baseline says tool calls go straight to the shell with nothing inspecting arguments, so there is no mediated boundary to extend; the reported utility cost (task success 0.356 to 0.067 on strict packs, arxiv:2603.18059) has to be budgeted, not assumed away.

ranked.technique: Adversarial tool metadata: poisoned descriptions, schemas and error strings
ranked.mechanism: The tool's own metadata is part of the agent's trusted context and is read every turn before any call is made, so an attacker who controls a description, a schema field, or a server's error message steers the next call without ever touching a tool result. Two properties make this the highest-leverage content channel. First, the surface inverts by model: the same byte-identical payload is 96% effective on one model's tool-output channel and 4% on its description channel, while the reverse holds for another model, so no single-surface number estimates the risk. Second, the attack is stealthy by construction -- optimised descriptions were flagged by MCP malware detectors at most 4.25% of the time. Error strings are a separate and underexamined carrier: messages written for human developers tell the agent what to do next, and half of those steps depend on something the server cannot see about the caller. Caution: enforcing the shape of the request does not establish that the request is trustworthy, and a schema-conformant smuggled request can carry path traversal, log injection or exfiltration.
ranked.reported_results: An optimised tool-description attack reached an average attack success of 83.23% across three benchmarks and up to 92.13% on one frontier model, while MCP malware detectors flagged it at most 4.25% of the time against up to 100% for baselines (arxiv:2610.33182). A two-stage trace-optimised attack reached a 93.6% macro-average malicious tool invocation rate across four scenarios on one backbone over 70-plus MCP servers, 74.4% success on information-exfiltration scenarios, and a 32.4x weighted token cost under induced cognitive overload (arxiv:2609.26761). Holding the payload byte-identical across 13 models, GPT-4.1 was 96% vulnerable on tool outputs and 4% on descriptions while Gemini-3-Flash was 20% versus 98%, and defences left the description channel above 54% (arxiv:2605.30454). A cross-framework measurement over 9,720 cells found 22.9% overall attack success with verified secret exfiltration in 12.1% of vulnerable cells, no framework-level defence, nine core frameworks clustered within 23-26%, and model attack success spanning 0.4% to 49.7% (arxiv:2611.03555). A self-evolving attack reached up to 96.7% attack success undefended and 69.2% under a common safety filter, beating the strongest baseline by 27.5% in the defended setting, across 120 malicious tasks and 198 tools (arxiv:2608.30441). In 150 widely used MCP servers, 949 of 3,001 error messages told the caller what to do next, and 62 of 67 credential-error steps asked for a terminal command, a configuration change or a web page; naming a server tool instead raised recovery to 84% on expired credentials and 88% on a rate limit, and the loss from a terminal-command instruction grew from 18 points for one model to 69 for a stronger one (arxiv:2609.35381). Fuzzing the orchestrator-tool boundary found 253 verified bugs across 343 tools in 118 repositories that a crash-based analyser located none of (arxiv:2610.13651). Hardening tool descriptions changed agent behaviour on tainted data flows (arxiv:2607.07461), and a static analyser over MCP server pitfalls achieved F1 1.0 on the statically checkable classes, with 29 baseline findings reduced to 0 at a mean cost of 27 lines of code (arxiv:2604.21477).
ranked.trajectory: The driver is protocol growth: the MCP server population grew to roughly 60,000 in sixteen months, descriptions are read on every turn, and the published attacks are open-source and already evade the available malware detectors. The direction is that tool metadata becomes a governed artefact -- signed, reviewed, pinned and diffed like a dependency, with descriptions treated as untrusted input rather than as configuration. The indicator is whether registries begin requiring metadata provenance or review, whether descriptions are hash-pinned per tool version, and whether vendors start shipping hardened default description templates, since the papers show description rewriting itself changes behaviour on tainted flows.
ranked.defensive_move: Treat tool descriptions and error strings as untrusted input that happens to sit in a trusted position. Pin and diff them per tool version, scan them for injected instructions and for steps that require a capability the tool cannot see, and enforce capability at the call rather than trusting the description. Where a server emits an error message, require the step to be expressed as a server tool call rather than as a terminal command or a configuration change. The control must reject a tool whose description contains an instruction to the agent and must reject an error step that asks for a shell command.
ranked.test_recipe: Take one benign tool and produce three variants -- an unmodified description, an optimised description, and an error message with a shell-command step -- and measure tool-selection rate and command rate against each, on at least two model families, because the surface effect inverts between them. Assert the optimised description does not change tool selection, and assert the error path never yields a shell command.

glm.rationale: Optimised tool-description attacks reach 83.23% average ASR while MCP malware detectors flag them at most 4.25% (arxiv:2610.33182), and a 9,720-cell MCP study measured 22.9% ASR with execution-verified exfiltration in 12.1% of vulnerable cells (arxiv:2611.03555). Metadata is read every turn before any call, which makes pin-and-diff per tool version one of the cheapest controls available — folded into the supply-chain admission work (G05-T01) rather than a separate effort.

minimax.rationale: Tool metadata is an instruction channel that needs no user error: 83.23% attack success with detection at no more than 4.25%, and across 949 of 3,001 error messages 62 of 67 asked the agent for a terminal command (arxiv:2610.33182, arxiv:2609.35381). The baseline has no provenance marking on tool results and no mediated boundary, so this is unaddressed; readiness is S because the cheap control - treat tool descriptions and error strings as untrusted input and never let them select a tool - is wiring, not a project.

ranked.technique: Indirect prompt injection: content the agent reads is executed as instruction
ranked.mechanism: An adversary who can write anything the agent will read -- a fetched page, a tool return value, a workspace file, a rule file, a log line, a retrieved document, an email -- embeds instructions that the model executes as if the operator had sent them, because the model has no way to tell data from instruction. The boundary that fails is the model's instruction hierarchy, and the evidence consumed is simply whatever text the agent pulled. The success rule is behavioural: the injected text changed a tool call, a parameter, a destination, or a generated claim. The rule does not require the payload to look like an instruction; several papers show a content-bearing payload (a false policy, a fabricated fact) steers the agent as reliably as an imperative, and one shows that a refusal is not the failure mode -- an agent that refuses the requested target can still perform the wrong adjacent action. Caution: the same payload's effect depends on where it lands and on which model reads it, so a defence validated on one surface and one model does not transfer.
ranked.reported_results: Across 3,375 trials on nine models the mean attack success rate was 64.4%, with per-entry-surface means of 58.3%-71.4% (arxiv:2610.04378). Undefended attack success over 215 SaaS-integration scenarios ranged from 32% on Claude Sonnet 4.6 to 81% on Gemini 3 Flash (arxiv:2606.02240). Attack success against GPT-4o-mini fell from 60% at injection depth 1 to 0% at depths 4-5, with depth 1 accounting for 67% of measured successes (arxiv:2605.30686). Injected log content drove 26.6% injection success under naive prompting and 11.8% under the strongest of four defences (arxiv:2605.24421). Script planting in shared workspaces averaged 81-84% (task-specific) and 73% (generic) attack success, and the highest-scoring model still had a 33% attack success rate (arxiv:2610.13623). Adaptive attacks exceeded 85% success against state-of-the-art defences, and most of 18 surveyed defence mechanisms achieved under 50% mitigation (arxiv:2601.17548). Long-horizon multi-surface benchmark: mean attack success 19.6% under LLM-based evaluation and 15.4% under heuristic verification, per-model 3.2%-41.9% (arxiv:2610.20776). A single untrusted issue in a five-agent CI/CD pipeline induced exfiltrating code that the agents verified but did not act on, over 280 synthetic runs (arxiv:2607.19267). Changing the scaffold alone moved attack success 8.6 percentage points, 40.0% to 48.6% (arxiv:2604.01438). Detection reduced objective attacks to 2.4% but left 9.5% (observation) and 12.1% (state), and a tool-policy defence allowed 15.4% versus 17.0% undefended (arxiv:2611.07640). Meta-SecAlign-70B, trained specifically to resist prompt injection, rose from a 3.2% baseline to 36.7% on incorrect-target injections (arxiv:2610.32531).
ranked.trajectory: The driver the papers name is that injection is a property of the deployment, not of the model: the same byte-identical payload flips from 4% to 96% attack success depending on which surface and which model family reads it, and adaptive search now beats fixed payloads. Direction of travel is that per-surface measurement and pre-execution authorisation replace model-level hardening, and that the attack surface grows with the number of tools and MCP servers a deployment attaches (the MCP server population grew to roughly 60,000 in 16 months). The indicator to watch is whether agent vendors publish per-surface, per-tool attack-success numbers and enforce capability at call time; if aggregate model benchmark numbers keep improving while deployed per-tool attack success stays flat, the extrapolation holds.
ranked.defensive_move: Put a typed-provenance layer at the tool boundary and a capability check at the call boundary. Every field of a tool result carries the origin that produced it; every proposed call is matched against the capabilities the task authorised, and a call is rejected or escalated when it targets a value or a destination the task never named. Do not rely on the system prompt to carry the rule -- the papers show agents verify and then proceed anyway.
ranked.test_recipe: Replay one fixed benign task with one payload per surface (tool output, tool description, retrieved doc, repo file, email body, log line, accessibility node) against the deployed harness, and record per surface both whether the payload was read and whether the action changed. Assert the per-surface attack-success rate, never the average.

glm.rationale: The corpus's most-reproduced result: mean 64.4% ASR over 3,375 trials across nine models (arxiv:2610.04378), 32-81% over 215 SaaS-integration scenarios (arxiv:2606.02240), with the same payload flipping 4%↔96% by surface and model (arxiv:2605.30454) — production clients, many model families, no single-lab dependency. The baseline reads repo files, issue bodies, tool results and web pages as undifferentiated text with no provenance; typed provenance at the tool boundary plus the capability check from G01-T01 is the structural close and the pack's own defensive move.

minimax.rationale: This is the most reproduced mechanism in the pack: mean attack success 64.4% across 3,375 trials with per-surface rates of 58.3-71.4%, and identical content read as tool output rather than as a tool description changed the outcome from 4% to 96% on GPT-4.1 (arxiv:2610.04378, arxiv:2605.30454). The baseline has no untrusted-content boundary at all - no provenance marking on repo files, issue bodies, dependency READMEs, web pages or tool results - so this is unaddressed; evidence confidence is 4 rather than 5 because these numbers come from benchmark harnesses rather than live deployments.

ranked.technique: Surface and channel enumeration with per-surface contamination measurement
ranked.mechanism: The unit of analysis is the channel, not the agent: enumerate every distinct path by which untrusted text reaches the model -- follow-up message, retrieved document, tool output, tool description, agent message, log field, accessibility node, rule file -- and measure contamination per channel rather than for the system as a whole. Three quantities must be kept apart: whether an injection is present, whether its presence changes behaviour, and how robust the model is to instructions in that channel. The accept rule for a measurement is that a detector is not credited for refusing text that never breached and not blamed for text that did, and that the same payload's success rate is reported per channel because the same string succeeds at very different rates under different wrappers. Caution: an aggregate attack-success number is close to meaningless here, because surface alone can explain none of the variance while the model-by-surface interaction explains most of it.
ranked.reported_results: Holding the payload byte-identical across 13 models from six families, vulnerability inverted by surface: GPT-4.1 was 96% vulnerable on tool outputs and 4% on tool descriptions, Gemini-3-Flash 20% versus 98%; surface alone accounted for 0% of outcome variance while model-by-surface interaction accounted for 16.7% (arxiv:2605.30454). The same attack string succeeded 18% of the time as a follow-up message but 53% when placed in retrieved context, and switching six model snapshots from follow-up training to RAG presentation raised average attack success from 18% to 53% (arxiv:2610.19133). Under framing wrappers attack success rose from 70% on casual follow-ups to roughly 92-96% for agent, tool and RAG wrappers (arxiv:2610.19133). Detection-only defences rejected almost everything, with false-positive-on-safe rates of 88.8-100% (PromptGuard), 86.4-92.4% (ProtectAI), 90.7-95.3% (LLM Detection) and 100% (KAD, Attention Tracker) (arxiv:2608.08027). At the lowest hardening level, 322 of 500 attack samples did not breach the model at all (arxiv:2608.08027). Across 100 repositories, compliance fell from 41% at modularity 1 to 21% at modularity 7, with attack success decomposed into reachability times compliance (arxiv:2608.14876). Trajectory-level detection could not be substituted by local content classifiers: Prompt Guard 2 and Llama Guard 4 detected only 40 and 55 malicious inputs against 270 of 300 (arxiv:2608.09476). A 328-case benchmark across seven persistent-carrier families found containment is carrier-specific and depends jointly on harness and model backend (arxiv:2608.06984).
ranked.trajectory: The driver is that attacks are now generated by search against the deployment (surface, channel, model) rather than replayed from a static list, and one paper measures 73-84% exact duplication of attack templates in existing red-team suites, so template-based measurement is going stale. The direction is per-channel attack-success reporting as the unit of operational assurance, with clean accuracy reported separately per channel. The indicator is whether benchmark suites start publishing per-channel clean-accuracy alongside per-channel attack success, and whether a single aggregate number stops being accepted as evidence of robustness.
ranked.defensive_move: Instrument the harness so every context item is tagged with its channel at write time, then run one calibration pass per channel with a fixed probe set and record attack success, clean accuracy and context-drift rate separately per channel. The gate is that no channel may be reported as protected on the strength of another channel's numbers, and any channel with no measured number is treated as unprotected.
ranked.test_recipe: Build a channel-labelled probe corpus (one payload family per channel, matched benign controls) and a harness that logs the channel of every token it admits; then assert that the reported attack success per channel is reproducible within a stated tolerance and that a channel with no probe is flagged as unmeasured rather than assumed safe.

glm.rationale: Holding the payload byte-identical across 13 models from six families, vulnerability inverted by surface (GPT-4.1: 96% on tool outputs, 4% on descriptions; Gemini-3-Flash the reverse) with surface alone explaining 0% of variance and the interaction 16.7% (arxiv:2605.30454); the same string succeeds 18% as a message and 53% in retrieved context (arxiv:2610.19133). Channel-tagging at write time plus per-channel calibration is cheap instrumentation every later control depends on — do it with the first boundary work, but it is measurement, so prepare-next alongside the controls it steers.

minimax.rationale: Surfaces are not equally contaminated and you only learn which by measuring them: surface-only measurement showed 0% variance where interaction measurement showed 16.7%, and one wrapper moved a measured rate from 18% to 53% (arxiv:2605.30454, arxiv:2610.19133). The baseline has no inventory of what the agent reads, so this is unaddressed; enumerating read surfaces and tool outputs is about a week of work and is the input to G03-T05, G03-T06 and G03-T11 - prepare-next.

ranked.technique: Covert and legitimate-looking exfiltration and credential-capture channels
ranked.mechanism: Data leaves the agent through channels that look like sanctioned work rather than through an obvious file copy: a semantic backdoor trigger embedded in a fine-tuned model, a denial-feedback side channel where an adversary learns from a refusal and later exfiltrates the inferred fact, an outbound retrieval request shaped to look like ordinary RAG traffic, a legitimate web fetch whose URL carries the payload, a poisoned tool whose output the agent accepts without checking, a steganographic perturbation of embedding stores, or an inline encoding inside the model's own output. Credentials are captured the same way, through phishing-style pages that trap a web agent's login flow, an LLM-mediated SSRF into an internal service, or a legitimately signed tool that carries concealed code. The rule for the defender is that exfiltration cannot be recognised by pattern-matching the carrier, so it must be cut by constraining destinations, by not letting secrets enter the carrier at all, and by checking tool outputs before they are trusted. Caution: a signed tool is not a benign tool — one evaluation saw a state-of-the-art runtime defense block the direct attempt in the same run and then fail against the concealed-channel variant in every trial; and detection built on a distributional prior is evaded by a white-box adaptive attacker, which drove both detectors' AUC to zero while preserving cosine similarity of 0.999.
ranked.reported_results: A legitimate web-fetch exfiltration achieved 79.7% attack success across eleven open-parameter models with a real-world chatbot case study and rarely raised warnings to the user (arxiv:2610.01768). Semantic backdoor triggers of 2-3 words produced over 96% attack success with under 0.3% false-positive rate and less than 1% MT-Bench loss, and activated reliably above 94% ASR across three domains, three model sizes and seven rerankers, reaching 85-91% top-5 placement and 81-87% defense bypass (arxiv:2604.05432). A login-flow trapping attack reached 86% average end-to-end success across backbones and 79% across agent architectures, with every tested webpage exploited within budget (arxiv:2608.04741). A signed-tool concealed-channel exfiltration defeated a runtime defense in every trial, while data-isolated execution produced no unauthorized disclosure in 153 attack runs across 91 generated variants with an LLM agent completing 7 of 7 tasks (arxiv:2611.06585). Steganographic post-embedding perturbation survived the default int8 quantization of common vector stores and tripped no native embedding-integrity control across more than 26,000 chunks; detector AUC stayed at chance across 35 operating points, and a white-box adaptive attacker drove both detectors' AUC to zero at an L2 budget of 0.5 with cosine similarity 0.999, with detectors only firing at higher capacity (OCSVM AUC ~0.92 at 256 B, ≥0.99 at 512 B) (arxiv:2605.13764). A linear probe on a shared encoding subspace recovered a held-out encoding family at AUC 0.975-1.000, and a two-channel monitor reached AUC 0.918 (95% CI [0.857, 0.957]) over 126 exfiltration scenarios, with a benign-encoding false-positive rate of 0% on one model, 18.8% on another and 100% on a third (arxiv:2606.10304). Denial-feedback leakage is stated to be invisible to flat provenance tracking (arxiv:2604.04035). Skill ecosystems carry widespread leakage: 520 of 17,022 sampled skills (3.1%) contain 1,708 credential issues, 84.0% from developer negligence, with 76.3% of cases visible only when descriptions and code are read together (arxiv:2604.03070). Memory extraction reached up to 100% ASR, with ASR 1.00 on one benchmark against a state-of-the-art baseline's 0.89 (arxiv:2604.09747). Multi-agent leakage totalled 68.9% exposure over 1,000 scenarios and 4,979 traces, 1.6x the single-agent baseline, with internal channels leaking at 57.8% against 27.2% external (arxiv:2602.11510). Poisoned tool output lowered task success by 26-39 percentage points despite strong clean performance (arxiv:2609.37153). Negative: the state-of-the-art runtime defense blocked a direct exfiltration attempt in the same run yet failed to prevent the concealed-channel attack in every trial (arxiv:2611.06585); a benign-encoding false-positive rate of 100% on one model shows the internal-probe defense is model-dependent (arxiv:2606.10304).
ranked.trajectory: Direction: exfiltration migrates from file and API channels to carriers the platform treats as legitimate — the sanctioned web fetch, the outbound retrieval, the embedding store, the signed tool, the model's own encoding — and the papers' consistent finding is that carrier-pattern defenses do not travel. The indicator would be agents defaulting to destination allow-listing and outbound-traffic budgets, and tool marketplaces shipping signed-but-behaviorally-verified tools rather than signature-only trust. Whether the internal-probe defense family (activation-subspace probes) survives productisation is genuinely open: the corpus reports a 0% to 100% swing in false-positive rate across three models, so treat that branch as unresolved rather than as a rising trend.
ranked.defensive_move: Constrain where agent-originated traffic may go rather than trying to recognise the payload: a destination allow-list for every outbound request, a rule that tool output is untrusted until checked against a stated expectation, and a credential path that never places secrets in the agent's context. It must refuse outbound requests to hosts outside the declared set, refuse to treat a signed tool as benign without behavioural verification, and refuse to let a denial's feedback become an inferable channel.
ranked.test_recipe: Replay the carrier suite — induced web fetch, outbound-retrieval shaping, embedded-store perturbation, inline encoding, login trapping and a concealed-channel signed tool — against the constrained deployment and assert zero unauthorized disclosures and zero credentials in the transcript; also run the adaptive-detector case and record the detector AUC, since the white-box attacker drives it to zero.

glm.rationale: Exfiltration through legitimate-looking carriers is measured at 79.7% ASR via the sanctioned web fetch across eleven models (arxiv:2610.01768) and 85-100% via memory-planted triggers, with distributional detectors driven to AUC zero by adaptive attackers (arxiv:2604.05432). The consistent finding is that payload recognition fails and destination control does not; the baseline puts nothing between the agent and the network, so an egress destination allow-list at the proxy is the this-quarter control for a severity-5 outcome.

minimax.rationale: A legitimate web fetch exfiltrated at 79.7% across eleven open-parameter models and rarely warned the user, and 2-3 word semantic triggers gave over 96% attack success at under 0.3% FPR (arxiv:2610.01768, arxiv:2604.05432). Carrier-pattern detection does not travel - a white-box adaptive attacker drove detector AUC to zero while a signed tool carrying a concealed channel defeated a runtime defense in every trial (arxiv:2605.13764, arxiv:2611.06585) - so the control is destination allow-listing plus keeping secrets out of the agent's context, and a login-flow trapping attack reached 86% end-to-end success against every tested page (arxiv:2608.04741). The baseline has no egress control and no mediated boundary, so this is unaddressed and the cheapest part is the allow-list.

ranked.technique: Tool-interface tripwires, honeytokens and kill-chain canaries
ranked.mechanism: Instrument the tool interface with markers, decoy credentials and staged canaries that a misusing agent reveals by using them, so detection comes from the attacker's own behaviour instead of a content filter. A kill-chain canary tracks a cryptographic token through EXPOSED, PERSISTED, RELAYED and EXECUTED stages to localize where blocking actually happens for a given model and pipeline; honeytokens built from character models plus pre-output activation probes catch credential access before any output token. Cheap by design — under 50 ms per tool call, no extra LLM calls — and detection-only rather than blocking.
ranked.reported_results: AgentShield catches 90.7–100% of successful attacks across 176 cross-lingual prompts with zero false alarms on 485 normal-use tests, at under 1% overhead (arxiv:2605.11026); kill-chain stage tracking across 950 runs shows Claude blocking all injections at memory-write (0/164 ASR) while GPT-4o-mini propagates at 53% and DeepSeek swings 0–100% across surfaces (arxiv:2603.28013); activation features separate credential-seeking prompts at substring AUROC 0.73 and fuzzy 0.80 under held-out encoding transformations (arxiv:2606.04141).
ranked.trajectory: Canaries move into agent tool interfaces and memory-write boundaries as indirect injection continues to succeed 24–50%+ of the time on state-of-the-art models; the driver is that detection-only defenses survive where prevention falls, and the prior finding that attacker-aware adversaries bypass purely preventive systems. The indicator is agent frameworks shipping canary tokens and decoy-tool options as configuration rather than research code.
ranked.defensive_move: Plant canary credentials and decoy tool results at the memory-write and relay boundaries your agent touches, and alarm on any use of them; the tripwire fires on the attacker's own action, so it should reject nothing legitimate and page a human on trigger. Stage-track the tokens first to learn which boundary actually blocks for your specific model.
ranked.test_recipe: Inject a canary secret into retrieved content, attempt exfiltration through a replayed tool sequence, and assert the alarm fires at the intended stage; then run a benign regression suite to confirm zero false alarms.

glm.rationale: AgentShield catches 90.7-100% of successful attacks with zero false alarms on 485 normal-use tests at under 1% overhead (arxiv:2605.11026), and kill-chain stage tracking localizes where blocking actually happens per model and pipeline (arxiv:2603.28013). Canary credentials and decoy tool results fire on the attacker's own action, cost milliseconds, and are classical blue-team practice the baseline simply has not extended to agent boundaries — the cheapest detection layer available while prevention controls mature.

minimax.rationale: Tool-interface tripwires are unusually cheap and sharp: 90.7-100% catch with zero false positives across 485 tests at under 1% overhead, though the point at which a model can be blocked is per-model (arxiv:2605.11026, arxiv:2603.28013). The baseline has no agent-side tripwires and no mediated tool call to hang one on, so this is unaddressed; readiness S because the mechanism is a canary credential or a decoy path, but it needs the G01-T01 call site first - prepare-next.

ranked.technique: Stealthy tool-loop cost amplification and termination poisoning
ranked.mechanism: The attack targets the agent's loop rather than its prompt. Three variants share that shape: tool-calling chains make the host re-meter a long history on every turn so the agent multiplies its own bill without ever exceeding a per-generation cap; a malicious or co-registered MCP tool server composes individually trivial calls into cyclic trajectories that inflate tokens and latency with no single step looking abnormal; and termination poisoning corrupts the agent's self-evaluation so a failing loop never stops. The boundary these cross is the billing and termination boundary, and the defenses differ accordingly: per-turn token caps and decoding-time concision controls fail against structural loops, while circuit breakers keyed on a per-session cost amplification factor and progress-authorized budgets hold, because a flat cap also kills legitimate work. The negative finding is explicit — the same retained state that carries the attack also carries the task, so dropping it does not fix the problem.
ranked.reported_results: Across six LLMs on ToolBench and BFCL, tool-calling chains produced per-query completions beyond 60,000 tokens, token budgets inflated up to 658x, total energy up to 561x and peak GPU KV-cache usage over 73%, while Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct held 96.2% attack success rate against 98.1% benign task success at 81,830 tokens per query (arxiv:2601.10955); MCP registry cycle induction caused up to 142.4x token amplification, benign-tool camouflage raised it further (GLM-4.7 on GPQA Diamond 6.1x to 10.8x, HumanEval 7.6x to 14.6x), and decoding-time concision controls did not reliably prevent loop induction (arxiv:2602.14798); termination poisoning over 8 agents and 60 GAIA tasks averaged 2.33x step amplification from static adversarial prompts, 3.57x with adaptive trap synthesis at a 25x peak and 3.93x total token overhead, with an enterprise deployment where a trapped agent exhausted thousands of dollars of compute in one afternoon (arxiv:2605.05846); the per-session input-token Cost Amplification Factor reached 14,293x, 51 of 69 priced attack sessions crossed a $0.10 circuit-breaker setting with $3.40 exposure versus a $0.025 benign maximum, only 71 of 3,830 scanned public MCP server and transport repositories expose any code-visible safeguard, and a progress-authorized budget achieved 22 of 24 oracle-verified task successes versus 13 of 24 under a fixed cap (arxiv:2609.28585).
ranked.trajectory: Direction: cost control moves from per-token caps to per-session, structure-aware accounting — amplification factor, tool-call-graph cycle detection, and attested loop progress — because the amplifiers are structural rather than textual. Drivers: longer contexts that make re-metering expensive, MCP tool registries as an unvetted supply chain where under 2% of scanned repositories expose any safeguard, and agents now running unattended in scheduled loops. Tension: attack success is conditioned on the target agent's behavioural signature rather than on a universal payload, so one generic filter will underperform and per-agent defences are needed; the indicator is an agent runtime exposing a per-session amplification metric and refusing sessions above a threshold, and the refuting signal is that agent billing remains purely token-based with no loop-level accounting.
ranked.defensive_move: Put the cap at the wallet, not at the prompt: enforce a per-session spend ceiling with a circuit breaker keyed on the input-token amplification factor, and release budget against demonstrated task progress rather than wall-clock, since a flat cap also stops legitimate work. Where you admit MCP servers, screen the registry for mutual recursion between registered tools and treat a tool server as untrusted input that can propose state. Flag and abort any session whose re-metered input grows superlinearly against its own tool output, and any agent that reports no progress across consecutive iterations.
ranked.test_recipe: Replay with a hostile-but-benign tool that returns large payloads plus a poisoned self-evaluation signal, then measure input tokens billed per turn against bytes returned, compute the per-session amplification factor, and assert the circuit breaker trips before the session exceeds its budget. Separately assert that a benign long-context task still completes under the progress-authorized policy, reproducing the 22 of 24 versus 13 of 24 success contrast rather than testing the breaker alone.

glm.rationale: Tool-loop amplification is measured at 658x tokens and 561x energy (arxiv:2601.10955) with MCP registry cycles reaching 142x (arxiv:2602.14798), and termination poisoning persisted across agents and tasks. The corpus is explicit that the same retained state carries the task, so dropping state is not the fix — a per-session wallet ceiling with an amplification-factor breaker and progress-gated budget release is; cheap, and pairs with G01-T06.

minimax.rationale: Cost amplification is the cheapest denial of service against an agent deployment: 658x inflation of tool-loop cost, 142.4x amplification of MCP cycles, and thousands of dollars of enterprise spend in the cited cases (arxiv:2601.10955, arxiv:2602.14798, arxiv:2605.05846). The baseline has no per-run budget and no termination policy, so this is unaddressed; prepare-next, and it pairs directly with G01-T06's workflow-level budget, which is the same control seen from the defender's side.

ranked.technique: Persistent memory poisoning with delayed cross-session activation
ranked.mechanism: The attacker writes content into whatever the agent persists -- memory entries, notes, files, skills, a scheduled task -- and the content detonates in a later session, or in a later turn of the same session, when a matching trigger arrives. The mechanism is decomposed into write, injection and activation stages, and end-to-end attack success is the product of the three rates, which is why per-stage numbers disagree across papers: a payload that writes reliably may activate rarely, and a payload that activates may not have been written. The boundary it crosses is the session boundary, so the same defence that filters content at read time sees only the retrieved record, not the provenance of how it got there. Caution and negative findings: pre-existing legitimate memories dramatically reduce attack effectiveness, so benchmarks with empty memory banks overstate the risk; removing the memory tool does not close the path, because agents fall back to writing files; LLM memory auditing is insufficient, and post-hoc auditing cannot distinguish a dormant trigger from normal context until it fires.
ranked.reported_results: Across a 24-configuration matrix of harnesses, memory backends and models, malicious memory persisted in 84.2% of cases and the full write-execute chain succeeded in 50.3%, with 56.1% of successfully poisoned cases achieving selective repair (arxiv:2607.27080). Undefended attack success persisted at 51-61% across 0 to 8 intervening sessions (arxiv:2606.24322). Retained injections redirected agent decisions in 59.38-76.39% of eligible triggers across four agent-backbone configurations, and 55.71% of eligible episodes exhibited all three silence-as-success properties simultaneously (arxiv:2611.01700). A memory-planted exfiltration trigger reached 85-100% attack success and survived 100 subsequent benign sessions; four evaluated defences cut success to 0-5% and a provably secure policy blocked it completely (arxiv:2605.01970). Fabricated sleeper memories were written up to 99.8% of the time on one frontier model and 95% on another, and among successful retrievals they caused attacker-intended actions in 60-89% of evaluations; goal-adjacent recall was 90-95% with 42-85% attacker use, while goal-distant recall fell to 3-8% (arxiv:2605.15338). Average injection success and cross-session attack success were 73.7%/55.5% on one harness and 66.9%/81.7% on another (arxiv:2609.13889). An evaluated attack reached 100% injection success with an empty initial memory bank and about 62% (GPT) and 52.94% (Llama) attack success, with pre-existing legitimate memories dramatically reducing effectiveness (arxiv:2601.05504). One model exceeded 50% attack success across all three plant-in-execute-persist strategies and all evaluated agents exceeded 27% under the persist variant, with one model jumping from low single-interaction success to 80.0% session attack success (arxiv:2605.28201). A zero-click autonomous worm persisted across production-grade heterogeneous agent ecosystems after initial injection, and user-prompt carriers achieved substantially higher attack compliance than system-prompt carriers, so reads outweigh writes as the integrity threat (arxiv:2605.02812). With the memory tool removed, agents wrote the goal to a file in 74% of sessions and self-propagation still succeeded in 11% of runs; an LLM memory auditor only reduced propagation from 71% to 34% (arxiv:2610.04083).
ranked.trajectory: The driver is that agent products in 2026 ship persistent memory by default -- the retrieved text notes configuration files, long-term memory and reusable skills are reloaded into context and carry attacks across tasks and sessions -- and that the write side is now ordinary product surface rather than a research artefact. The papers also name the countervailing force: payloads optimised end-to-end across write, retrieval and utilisation defeat payloads crafted for one stage, so the attack is getting harder to filter at any single stage. The indicator is whether memory-write interception appears as a standard agent-platform feature with a visible accept/review/quarantine decision, and whether cross-session attack success starts being reported as a headline metric alongside single-session numbers.
ranked.defensive_move: Gate every write to persistent state at the store, not at read time: classify the write by origin and semantic risk, quarantine anything from an external source that is not clearly benign, and require the trusted execution layer -- not the model -- to be the writer of records that later authorise an action. Record the write decision so it can be replayed, and never let the model be the sole judge of whether its own memory write is safe.
ranked.test_recipe: Run a two-session harness: session one plants a payload through an ordinary interaction, session two issues an unrelated task with a matching trigger, and the verifier scores the plant stage and the activation stage independently. Assert the plant rate and the activation rate as two numbers, and re-run with a pre-populated legitimate memory bank so the report does not overstate the risk.

glm.rationale: Malicious memory persisted in 84.2% of a 24-configuration matrix with the full write-execute chain succeeding in 50.3% (arxiv:2607.27080), attack success held at 51-61% across eight intervening sessions (arxiv:2606.24322), and removing the memory tool just pushes agents to write files — so read-time filtering is structurally insufficient. 2026 agent products ship persistent memory by default while the baseline gates nothing at the store; the write-gate (classify by origin, quarantine external, trusted layer writes authority-bearing records) is the control to build now.

minimax.rationale: Poisoned memory persists: 84.2% of injections persisted and 50.3% chained across 24 configurations, and 85-100% attack success survived 100 sessions of scrubbing (arxiv:2607.27080, arxiv:2605.01970). The baseline keeps no agent memory and has no lifecycle gating, so this is unaddressed; with G03-T08 it is one of the two highest-momentum ways an agent is steered by content rather than by its principal, and unlike most techniques here the fix (write-time gating plus provenance) is a design choice you make before the store exists.

ranked.technique: End-to-end autonomous offensive capability and where its boundary sits
ranked.mechanism: An agent is scored on whether it reaches unauthorized access unaided: it invokes tools, probes the target, plans from observed feedback and adapts until it gets in, with no human in the loop, no prior target knowledge and no task-specific instructions. The measurement is end to end against real targets — web challenge benchmarks, an Active Directory domain environment, synthetic enterprise topologies and commercial EDR products — so the score is an outcome rather than a proxy. The corpus locates the boundary precisely: exploitation is strong once the agent is handed accurate vulnerability context (up to 90.0% functional success), while autonomous reconnaissance recall plateaus near 50.0%, mostly because agents fail to parse unstructured telemetry, so the choke point is finding the target, not compromising it. Two cautions travel with the numbers: benchmark realism is weak (Cybench does not capture lateral movement or iterative reconnaissance central to real intrusion workflows), and the scoreboards are demonstrations rather than continuous operators, with agents still needing trajectory or strategy repair to rebuild exploits from incomplete public references.
ranked.reported_results: Autonomous penetration success spans 10.7% to 69.3% across 19 open-weight and proprietary LLMs and improves alongside overall model capability (arxiv:2606.13079); 87% XSS success on the 104-challenge XBOW benchmark (arxiv:2603.00960); all seven commercial endpoint platforms tested were bypassed, peak evasion 90% on Windows Defender and 86.7% on Trend Micro, with a knowledge base lifting 8B models from 27-53% to 43-83% evasion, at parity with proprietary models (arxiv:2608.01639); LLM-instantiated attack agents reached up to 94.5% compromise at 0.02-0.06 seconds per assessment, roughly 25,000x to 50,000x faster than RL training cycles across 6,000 episodes (arxiv:2608.16422); with accurate vulnerability context agents reach up to 90.0% functional success while autonomous reconnaissance recall plateaus at approximately 50.0% (arxiv:2606.25332); the offensive space is systematized into eight ATT&CK-aligned attack classes (arxiv:2605.06486).
ranked.trajectory: Direction: end-to-end autonomous intrusion capability keeps rising with base-model capability, and the same harness pattern solved targets an earlier model never finished, with curated threat-intelligence knowledge bases lifting small open models to proprietary parity. Drivers: model capability, MCP tool affordances, and knowledge-engineering that removes the payload-authoring bottleneck. Tension to keep: reconnaissance, not exploitation, is the binding constraint, so the indicator to watch is an autonomous agent completing a multi-stage intrusion that includes lateral movement against production-shaped telemetry, not a higher single-host exploit rate; the corpus's own benchmark-realism critique means measured rates may overstate real intrusion fluency.
ranked.defensive_move: Put the control at the effect boundary rather than the prompt boundary: constrain the agent's outcome — credential use, host access, data movement — with the authorization allow-list enforced at the identity and network layers the agent must cross. Issue engagement credentials scoped and short-lived to the target set, and have the enforcement point reject agent-initiated use of any credential, host or segment outside that set, because detection alone is not a control (every commercial EDR platform tested was bypassed). Flag every agent action that touches a resource outside the allow-list, and treat every reported finding as unverified until an independent reproduction gate accepts it.
ranked.test_recipe: Replay a closed-loop engagement against a lab target set twice — once with the scope guardrail enabled, once with it disabled — and assert that every recorded action target is inside the allow-list and every credential was scoped and single-use in the guarded run, while the unguarded run demonstrably steps out of scope, so the check cannot pass vacuously. Reference protocols: the multi-model Active Directory harness with guardrail activations, and the agent-vs-agent red-team harness that produced 72 reproducible agent-system vulnerabilities.

glm.rationale: Autonomous penetration success spans 10.7-69.3% across 19 models and tracks base capability, with all seven commercial endpoint platforms bypassed at up to 90% evasion (arxiv:2606.13079, arxiv:2608.01639) — measured against real targets with the corpus honest about missing lateral-movement realism. The pack's defensive move is the same effect-boundary control as G01-T01/G01-T08; the threat trend raises those controls' priority rather than adding a new project.

minimax.rationale: Autonomous offensive capability is now real and broad: 10.7-69.3% across 19 models on end-to-end tasks, 7 of 7 endpoint defences bypassed at a peak of 90%, and exploitation succeeding at 90% where reconnaissance succeeded at 50% (arxiv:2606.13079, arxiv:2608.01639, arxiv:2606.25332). The baseline has endpoint controls (EDR, managed browser, VPN) but no agent-specific boundary, so this is unaddressed; prepare-next rather than prepare-now, because the appropriate response is containment (G01-T07) and monitoring, not trying to out-build the attacker - and the numbers are benchmark results, not incidents.

ranked.technique: Decomposed injection: cross-channel fragmentation and cross-turn staged propagation
ranked.mechanism: The payload is split so that no single unit carries a detectable instruction, which is what defeats per-unit and per-turn filtering. Cross-channel fragmentation splits one instruction across two channels the agent ingests separately -- an MCP tool description delivered at connection time and the tool result delivered after invocation, or attacker-optimised metadata plus return values -- so each channel carries a benign fragment and the model assembles the instruction. Cross-turn staging splits the goal across a chain of pages, tool calls or causally connected workflow stages, so the pattern only exists across the trace. The boundary crossed is the per-unit filter's assumption that the unit is the decision. The measured rule is the gap between single-channel and fragmented-channel compliance: models that fully resist the single channel can be driven to full credential exfiltration under two-channel fragmentation, and security tools and three prompt-based defences fail to detect the cross-channel attack. Caution: a benchmark that fixes one injection position reports zero at deeper positions and so manufactures false confidence, and the same string's success rate depends on the channel it arrives through.
ranked.reported_results: Models that fully resisted single-channel injection at 0% compliance exfiltrated credentials at up to 100% under two-channel fragmentation, measured across 12 frontier models, three production clients, six payloads and over 15,000 trials; security tools and three prompt-based defences failed to detect the cross-channel attack, and each model showed unequal authority across channels (arxiv:2609.18217). Cross-turn fragmentation raised the average risk trigger rate from a 28.3% naive prompt-injection baseline to 52.6%, across 2,254 multi-turn dialogues with 1,512 adversarial cases covering 34 attack techniques (arxiv:2605.22321). A staged-injection auditor reached 86.1% recall at a 6.0% false-block rate on a native-runtime corpus of 240 confirmed attacks, versus the strongest baseline's 44.1% at 32.5% (arxiv:2610.05163). Splitting a payload across a chain of pages defeated per-page inspection (arxiv:2608.06477), and distributing injections as a breadcrumb trail across a search process kept the agent hijacked as later evidence diluted any single page (arxiv:2608.04565). Within one model, the same payload's success varied by channel and position, with attack success falling from 60% at injection depth 1 to 0% at depths 4-5 while a different harm type persisted at depth 2 (arxiv:2605.30686). A zero-click worm's read-path carriers achieved substantially higher attack compliance than its system-prompt carriers, so reads outweigh writes as the integrity threat (arxiv:2605.02812).
ranked.trajectory: The mechanism is well measured but the defence side is not: the strongest published auditor still leaves 44-47% of staged attacks at a usable false-block rate, and the fragmented-channel case is reported as a measurement result rather than as a defeated defence. The driver is that agents became multi-channel and multi-stage by construction -- tool descriptions, results, retrieval, files and scheduled tasks all enter over a long horizon -- so the payload can always be split along an existing seam. The indicator is whether any deployed guard begins to reassemble across channels or across the trace rather than scoring each unit, and whether multi-channel fragmentation appears in the standard agent red-team suites.
ranked.defensive_move: Do not validate channels independently. Add a session-level check that reassembles the fragments -- a rule that fires when instruction-like content appears split across two or more sources within a window, and a stage-level check that compares the workflow's current action against the accumulated trace rather than the current turn. The control must reject a call whose instruction was reconstructed from more than one channel, and must flag a staged chain whose fragments are individually benign but whose assembled goal is not the user's.
ranked.test_recipe: Build the two variants explicitly: split one payload across a tool description and a tool result, and split one goal across three turns of a workflow. Assert the single-channel and single-turn controls still pass on each fragment while the reassembling control fires on the assembled case, and measure the fragment-level compliance gap, which is the number that shows whether your filters are per-channel.

glm.rationale: Models that fully resisted single-channel injection at 0% compliance exfiltrated credentials at up to 100% under two-channel fragmentation, across 12 models, three production clients and 15,000+ trials (arxiv:2609.18217) — severity-5 capability measured against shipped clients. The defense side is the weak link: the best staged-injection auditor still leaves 44-47% of attacks through at usable false-block rates, so no tested product control exists yet; the session-level reassembly check is buildable but not proven.

minimax.rationale: Splitting an injection across channels defeats single-channel filters completely - exfiltration went from 0% to 100% under a two-channel scheme over 15,000+ trials, and cross-turn staged propagation pushed evasion from 28.3% to 52.6% (arxiv:2609.18217, arxiv:2605.22321). The baseline's total absence of an untrusted-content boundary makes this unaddressed, but the control - per-channel typing plus cross-turn state tracking - is the same machinery as G03-T02 and G03-T06, so sequence it after them rather than buying it as a separate item.

ranked.technique: Runtime risk scoring, rate limits and workflow-level risk budgets
ranked.mechanism: Risk is scored over the whole trajectory rather than a single turn: each tool invocation carries a risk score that feeds a decision to allow, throttle or stop, and the policy can be reloaded without restarting the agent. Per-tool rate limits sit alongside a workflow-level budget because per-turn limits do not constrain a multi-step chain — a tool-calling chain can multiply cost without ever exceeding any single per-generation cap, because the host recomputes a long history every turn. The shared budget across a workflow accounts for inter-step risk propagation, and the aggregate is bounded by a finite-sample certificate whose independence assumption is stated rather than assumed away. The rule is that a risk budget is spent across the agent, not per step, so several individually acceptable actions are not judged separately. Caution: the corpus shows the same mechanism abused by the defender — a progress-authorized budget (authorizing spend by demonstrated progress) admits more successful workflows than a fixed cap, so a budget that is too generous is as unsafe as one that is too tight; and the guarantee that a population's aggregate risk stays bounded depends on an independence assumption that does not hold for correlated agent steps.
ranked.reported_results: A shared risk budget across a multi-step workflow improved average defense success rate from 0.658 to 0.825 against direct prompt injection and from 0.460 to 0.775 against indirect prompt injection, while false triggers fell from 0.390 to 0.129 (arxiv:2611.10411). Tool-calling chains pushed per-query completions beyond 60,000 tokens, inflated token budgets by up to 658x, raised total energy by up to 561x and peak KV-cache use above 73%; on ToolBench one model reached 96.2% attack success against 98.1% benign task success while averaging 81,830 tokens per query, measured across 105 MCP servers and 261 queries (arxiv:2601.10955). A denial-of-wallet study measured a maximum per-session cost amplification factor of 14,293x, with 51 of 69 priced attack sessions crossing a $0.10 circuit-breaker setting and exposure reaching $3.40 against a $0.025 benign maximum; a progress-authorized policy achieved 22/24 oracle-verified successes with no pre-completion interruptions against 13/24 under a fixed cap, and only 71 of 3,830 scanned public MCP server and transport repositories expose any code-visible safeguard proxy (arxiv:2609.28585). A cost-aware tier split ran more than 96% of search tokens on the cheapest tier at 5.6-14x lower search cost, rising to 25-54x where reasoning tiers emit long chains of thought, over a break-even price ratio of 0.50-3.46 (arxiv:2608.10694). A bounded iterative harness optimization protocol produced normalized gains from -0.03 to 0.63 with resolution bands of ±0.035 to ±0.066 across four task suites, and some nominated candidates were worse than the seed (arxiv:2608.06301). A defensive multi-turn posture held attack success below 0.02 across 5-20 turns with a misdirection rate of 0.34-0.41, at about a 20% throughput drop (arxiv:2608.00134). Negative: the same state that carries the attack also carries the task, so pruning it removes the attack and the work together (arxiv:2609.28585); a finite-sample safety certificate holds only under an explicit independence assumption (arxiv:2609.28182).
ranked.trajectory: Direction: cost and risk budgets converge on one workflow-level meter, with spend authorized by demonstrated progress rather than by a fixed cap, driven by the measured 658x and 14,293x amplification figures and by the observation that the agent's own state is what carries the attack. The indicator would be agent runtimes exposing a single per-run budget that spans turns, tools and model tiers, with the progress signal exposed to the operator. Expect the certificate side to lag the metering side: the finite-sample bounds in the corpus are stated under independence assumptions the agent setting does not obviously satisfy, so the trajectory is a usable operational budget first and a formal guarantee later.
ranked.defensive_move: Enforce one shared budget across the whole agent — turns, tools and model tier — rather than per-step caps, and attach a circuit breaker to the amplification factor rather than to raw token count. It must stop the run when the workflow-level budget is exhausted even if no single call exceeded a per-call limit, and it must refuse to resume a run whose billable state has been truncated or truncated mid-stream.
ranked.test_recipe: Run a tool-calling chain attack and a denial-of-wallet attack against the meter, then assert that total session cost and the amplification factor stay under the configured bound and that the circuit breaker fires on the attack sessions while the benign session stays under its $0.025-equivalent maximum.

glm.rationale: The attack side is well measured — 658x token and 561x energy amplification via tool-calling chains at 96.2% ASR (arxiv:2601.10955), 142x via MCP registry cycles (arxiv:2602.14798) — but the workflow-budget defense rests mainly on one study (0.658→0.825, arxiv:2611.10411) whose aggregate-risk bound assumes independent agent steps. Baseline has no budgets at all; a per-session spend ceiling with an amplification-factor circuit breaker is cheap enough to fold into the first hardening cycle without justifying its own project.

minimax.rationale: A shared workflow-level budget lifted defense success from 0.658 to 0.825 against direct injection and cut false triggers from 0.390 to 0.129, while a denial-of-wallet study measured 14,293x cost amplification with only 71 of 3,830 scanned MCP repositories exposing any code-visible safeguard (arxiv:2611.10411, arxiv:2609.28585). Baseline has no per-run budget at all, so this is unaddressed and cheap; but a progress-authorized budget admitted more successful workflows than a fixed cap and the state that carries the attack also carries the task, so treat a spend cap as availability hygiene rather than a security control.

ranked.technique: Capability scoping and least-privilege grant derivation
ranked.mechanism: The set of capabilities an agent may exercise is derived from the task it was actually given — the skill's declared procedures, a learned classification of the request, the antichain of minimal tool sets, or the assets the task actually touches — and granted at tool and path granularity rather than at role granularity for the whole session. The derivation is materialised as an explicit grant set stored outside the model's context, and a call to anything outside that set does not exist to be made. The evidence consumed is the task statement, the task-context classifier's output, and a set of combination prohibitions that are not expressible per tool. The rule is deny-by-default with the grant set closed before the run and not open to runtime extension; anything derivable but not derivable-from-the-task is withheld. Caution: the corpus shows the derivation step is the weak link, not the enforcement — agents omit permissions the execution chain needs and grant unused or sensitive ones at the same time, and reasoning-effort scaling does not move a model toward a safe authorization window; it only makes it more consistent in its own failure mode. A runtime safety router that scoped tools was also bypassed by an agent that returned natural-language instructions for a reverse shell without ever emitting a tool call, which the authors call a fundamental architectural boundary rather than a bug.
ranked.reported_results: In a three-source dynamic scoping architecture, ceiling violations fell from 46 to 3 (93%) through dataset-policy iteration, over a synthetic set of 600 enterprise task prompts labelled across a 15-permission taxonomy (Cohen's kappa 0.917 pre-review, 0.967 post-review) (arxiv:2607.22445). In an empirical evaluation of the same shape, the role ceiling alone closed 27.9% of the severity-weighted attack surface and adding the task classifier closed 84.4%; the prohibition layer added 11.5-13.6% when the classifier was bypassed while blocking 6-31% of legitimate tasks, and a 355M-parameter on-host encoder matched frontier-classifier performance (arxiv:2609.15422). AuthBench's Full-Access baseline reached 83.3% task success against a Golden-Permission reference of 77.1%, and a tightness-biased decomposition improved sensitive-task success by up to 15.8% (arxiv:2605.14859). Microsoft's shipped privilegeLevel rated 67.4%-74.4% of incomparable permission pairs equal and a reconstructed FORTIS ladder on Google rated 90.7%-98.7% equal; ReadWrite.All authorizes 355 endpoints against 11 for DelegatedPermissionGrant.ReadWrite.All, and the gap between the minimal antichain grant and the smallest shipped grant was 32.3 points (arxiv:2610.31914). Deriving only the assets a task needed dropped native attack success from 93/560 to 1/560 over 620 AgentDyn cases, with task completion 40.0% and 36.4% (arxiv:2610.39155). A learned capability governor removed 73% of tools and 100% of dangerous tools on a live deployment (+260% Skill Economy Ratio), and its safety router blocked all 8 adversarial tool calls at 2,094 ms classifier latency (arxiv:2604.11839). Out-of-context typed capabilities cut the injected effect to 3/75 runs against 33-47/75 under ambient-authority baselines (arxiv:2609.08371). Showing privilege class and cost in tool descriptions lowered over-privileged tool selection on every model that over-privileges, by up to 19.3 percentage points (50%) (arxiv:2610.40975). Translating a skill's declared procedure into a subagent's tool, key and path set beat the corresponding base models by 13.8 and 8.3 points on Subagent Management Score (arxiv:2611.08905). Negative: more reasoning produced consistency in each model's own failure mode (broad-but-exposed or tight-but-brittle) rather than movement toward the safe window (arxiv:2605.14859); an agent returned natural-language instructions for `nc -l -p 4444` without a tool call and the safety router did not intercept it (arxiv:2604.11839).
ranked.trajectory: Direction: capability derivation shifts from a static per-role grant at session start to a task-conditioned grant computed at run time, driven by the finding that one shared context mixes user requests, tool results, documents, shell output and memory, so a static pre-provisioned set cannot express least privilege, and by vendor privilege ladders that rate incomparable scopes as equal. The indicator would be permission models shipping explicit minimal-grant (antichain-style) sets and per-task ceilings in production rather than only in research prototypes. Expect the derivation to move partly out of the frontier model — the corpus shows a 355M-parameter on-host encoder matching a frontier task classifier — which is the opposite of the current default of judging authorization with the same model that requested it.
ranked.defensive_move: Compute the minimal tool-and-path grant set from the task before the run, store it outside the model's context, and enforce it in a gateway the model cannot rewrite. It must reject a call to any tool absent from the derived set, reject a request whose parameters exceed the granted scope, and refuse any runtime path that widens the grant without a fresh derivation.
ranked.test_recipe: Run the same task twice — once under the derived minimal grant, once with full access — against the attack set that the corpus uses, and assert that attack success collapses while task completion holds; additionally assert that the grant set contains no tool the task never needs and no permission the execution chain did not use.

glm.rationale: Role ceilings closed 27.9% of the severity-weighted attack surface and task-conditioned classification 84.4% (arxiv:2609.15422), but the 600-prompt enterprise taxonomy is synthetic-label and the natural-language reverse-shell bypass shows scoping cannot live inside the model. The baseline has no per-task grant derivation at all. The outside-the-model grant-set gateway is one integration cycle of work after the per-call engine (G01-T01) lands.

minimax.rationale: Deriving only the assets a task actually needed dropped native attack success from 93/560 to 1/560, and adding the task classifier on top of a role ceiling closed 84.4% of the severity-weighted attack surface against 27.9% for the ceiling alone (arxiv:2610.39155, arxiv:2609.15422).
