The deployable fragment — risk-conditioned admission with typed assurance obligations and refusing the unresolved case — is sound design vocabulary for the G01 controls rather than a separate mechanism.

minimax.rationale: Mechanism design for agent ecosystems is not deployable evidence: escalation recall moved 0 to 0.67 on a sample of 12, the risk-conditioned admission work ran 2,730 trials, and repeated games show the incentive failing over time (arxiv:2609.37501, arxiv:2609.16313, arxiv:2608.09055). Severity 2, readiness L, evidence confidence 2, and the owner is the regulator - skip for this planning cycle, and revisit only with a concrete multi-agent market in view. The baseline's agent deployment involves no multi-party marketplace, so there is no incentive to design for.

ranked.technique: Topology confidentiality via behavior-preserving obfuscation
ranked.mechanism: The communication topology of a multi-agent system encodes domain knowledge and workflow design, and inference attacks can reconstruct it from agent outputs (edge-level F1 above 0.87), leaking IP and aiding targeted attacks. The defense injects fake edges and fake messages selected for low impact, preserving output-distribution equivalence and task-accuracy non-inferiority, with fake edges indistinguishable under black-box observation. The boundary held is the observable channel: the attacker keeps the outputs but loses the graph, and behavior preservation is the accept rule — obfuscation that changed outputs would be self-defeating.
ranked.reported_results: Topology-inference edge-level F1 reduced from >0.87 to 0.62 and graph similarity from >0.94 to 0.71, with task-accuracy non-inferiority and fake edges indistinguishable under black-box observation (arxiv:2611.00923).
ranked.trajectory: Grows only if workflow-graph IP becomes a recognized asset and topology-inference attacks are demonstrated against real deployments; the driver is the value of workflow design itself. The indicator is obfuscation overhead and equivalence numbers quoted outside the original paper — currently absent from this corpus.
ranked.defensive_move: If the workflow graph is sensitive, enable behavior-preserving obfuscation (fake edges and messages) and verify output equivalence before making it permanent. Treat published traces and demos as topology leaks, the way teams treat credentials in logs.
ranked.test_recipe: Run a topology-inference attack against obfuscated vs plain logs; require the F1 drop with task accuracy inside the non-inferiority band.

glm.rationale: Topology inference reaches edge-level F1 above 0.87 and obfuscation reduces it to 0.62 with task-accuracy non-inferiority (arxiv:2611.00923) — one careful paper. Workflow-graph IP becomes worth defending only if the team's multi-agent topology is itself the competitive asset; the cheap half (treating published traces and demos as topology leaks) is a documentation rule.

minimax.rationale: Topology confidentiality through behaviour-preserving obfuscation is not yet strong: F1 fell from above 0.87 to 0.62 (arxiv:2611.00923). Severity 2, momentum 2, evidence confidence 2, and the baseline has no multi-agent topology to hide in the first place - skip.

ranked.technique: Calibrated privacy auditing of model artifacts
ranked.mechanism: Audits of what a released model actually retains: conformal re-identification combines LLM re-identification with auxiliary knowledge while attaching finite-sample statistical guarantees to the audit outcome, because pipeline success rates say nothing about individual documents and training-time protections like differential privacy do not translate to release-time decisions. Probabilistic per-document training-data extraction controls for model-free blind baselines that confound aggregate membership-inference AUC, and information-theoretic defenses replace heuristic perturbations against prompt inversion from shared activations in collaborative inference. The retrieved evidence states methods and guarantees but no numeric results.
ranked.maturity: research — method papers without deployment; the attacks they calibrate (re-identification, extraction, prompt inversion) are the same primitives measured numerically elsewhere in this group (see T12).
ranked.trajectory: Calibrated audits with statistical guarantees become the standard by which 'private enough to release' is argued, as aggregate MIA scores are shown confounded by blind baselines; the indicator is a release process requiring a finite-sample per-document bound rather than an aggregate score. Kept in this group because uncalibrated audits produce false confidence — a negative finding about current practice.
ranked.defensive_move: Before shipping a fine-tune on sensitive corpora, run a per-document probabilistic extraction audit with a blind baseline and treat any document above the significance threshold as a recall; do not accept aggregate membership-inference metrics as clearance.
ranked.test_recipe: Hold out a canary document set, measure per-document recovery significance against the blind baseline, and assert the conformal bound is met before each release.

glm.rationale: The pack itself flags that the retrieved evidence states methods and guarantees with no numeric results, and only three papers back it. The underlying attacks (re-identification, extraction) are real primitives measured elsewhere, but as a distinct front this is the thinnest entry in the supply-chain group; keep on radar for teams releasing fine-tunes on sensitive corpora, nothing more.

minimax.rationale: Privacy auditing of model artefacts is not yet a usable technique: the corpus records no numeric results for the member-inference approach and notes the measurement is confounded (arxiv:2606.11592, arxiv:2609.21340). Readiness is L, the owner is the model provider, and evidence confidence is 2 - watch, and do not plan a privacy control on this basis. The baseline keeps no model-artifact privacy posture, so there is nothing here to extend.

ranked.technique: Causal credit attribution and compromised-peer tolerance in training
ranked.mechanism: Two structural answers to a compromised peer, both on the training side rather than the prompt: attribute a shared safety violation back to the agents whose actions most strongly caused it, using signal-temporal-logic robustness with differentiable dynamics for per-agent credit assignment; and keep each agent's data and training state local, reaching agreement over distributed communication, so no central trainer aggregates every trajectory and a compromised peer measurably loses leverage. The boundary held is the trust domain — no single aggregation point needs to see everything, which is also what lets training span devices and organizations. Note the evidence is from classic multi-agent RL settings (transport, navigation, traffic), not yet LLM agent pipelines.
ranked.reported_results: STL-robustness credit assignment achieved 1.6-5.1x the safe-success rate in transport, improved navigation safe-success by 11.1%, and delivered 50-68% more throughput in traffic versus constrained baselines (arxiv:2610.13737); under compromised-agent settings, the decentralized scheme reduced HarmBench attack success rate by up to 26.4% while achieving reasoning gains comparable to centralized training (arxiv:2610.24380).
ranked.trajectory: The driver the papers name is data sovereignty — training across devices and trust domains without a common trainer — which keeps decentralized schemes relevant independently of security. The indicator is an LLM-agent framework citing ADMM-style agreement or STL-robustness attribution; nothing of that kind appears in this corpus, so cross-over is unproven.
ranked.defensive_move: When agents train jointly, avoid a central aggregator that sees every trajectory — keep data local with agreement over distributed communication, which measurably blunts a compromised peer. At runtime, attribute shared violations causally so the culprit agent is named rather than the whole team being flagged.
ranked.test_recipe: Compromise one agent during training and compare attack-success deltas centralized vs decentralized; on a synthetic shared violation, require the attribution layer to name the causing agent.

glm.rationale: The decentralized-training result (up to 26.4% ASR reduction under a compromised agent) comes from classic multi-agent RL settings — transport, navigation, traffic — not LLM agent pipelines, as the pack itself notes (arxiv:2610.24380). Relevant only if the team ever trains agents jointly across trust domains; keep the no-central-aggregator principle in mind.

minimax.rationale: Compromised-peer tolerance in training is studied only in classic multi-agent RL settings - transport, navigation and traffic - with no agentic counterpart in the corpus (arxiv:2610.13737, arxiv:2610.24380). Severity 2, momentum 2, evidence confidence 2, and the owner is whoever trains the model - skip, and revisit only if the team trains multi-agent models rather than deploying them. The baseline deploys models it does not train, so this is out of the team's reach.

ranked.technique: Economic anti-collusion mechanisms (report-and-penalise)
ranked.mechanism: Spontaneous collusion among embodied agents manifests as subtle coordinated deviation from intent, which identity control and post-hoc behavior analysis miss because physical feedback is delayed and noisy. The intervention is payoff-shaping: a report-and-penalise mechanism with refundable reporting deposits, smart-contract reward enforcement, and encrypted anonymous reporting makes defection the dominant strategy, giving collusion a cost instead of relying on detecting it. The boundary held is the incentive boundary around each agent, and enforcement is auditable — smart-contract execution costs roughly $0.30 per action.
ranked.reported_results: The mechanism effectively suppressed collusion by inducing defection, achieving performance comparable to the non-collusion baseline and outperforming representative reactive defences (arxiv:2604.23511); smart-contract execution incurred approximately 94,700 gas, about $0.30 (arxiv:2604.23511).
ranked.trajectory: Stays research-bound unless agents begin transacting under verifiable contracts, since the mechanism presumes on-chain enforcement of rewards and penalties. The indicator would be a multi-agent platform reporting a deployed report-and-penalise scheme; none appears in this corpus.
ranked.defensive_move: Where agents share real rewards (embodied or economic settings), add a report-and-penalise layer with refundable whistleblower deposits and anonymous encrypted reporting so that defection from collusion pays. It must sit in the reward/contract layer — penalising confirmed collusion and refunding reporters judged honest — not in the model.
ranked.test_recipe: Simulate a colluding group under the mechanism; require defection to emerge and group performance to recover to the non-collusion baseline.

glm.rationale: A single paper whose mechanism presumes on-chain enforcement of rewards and penalties at ~$0.30 per action (arxiv:2604.23511), with the trajectory note conceding no multi-agent platform reports a deployed report-and-penalise scheme anywhere in this corpus. Embodied agents transacting under verifiable contracts is not a 12-36 month scenario for a baseline team; skip until the precondition exists.

minimax.rationale: Economic anti-collusion mechanisms operate at the smart-contract scale at $0.30 per action (arxiv:2604.23511). Severity 2, momentum 2, evidence confidence 2, and there is no analogue to an internal agent deployment - skip for this planning cycle, and revisit only if a multi-agent marketplace with real economic stakes is in scope. The baseline runs no multi-party economic agent market, so there is no anti-collusion incentive to install.
